item.content:encoded:
1566 points · View discussion

Top Comments

💬 Many people report seeing this behavior when using the SEC API specifically which makes me think that service is requesting this. Maybe email is required by the SEC API?

---

UPDATE: The SEC API documentation requires your email in the User-Agent and will reject you otherwise. Demo:

    U='https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyconcept/CIK0000320193/us-gaap/Assets.json'
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'response: %{http_code}  curl default User-Agent, rejected\n'  "$U"
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'response: %{http_code}  email in user-agent, success\n' -A 'Acme Research admin@acme-research.example' "$U"

    response: 403  curl default, rejected
    response: 200  email in user-agent, success
SEC docs: https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/edgar-search-assistance/a...

So basically Claude is trying to problem solve, and just does what the SEC asks. It's a 'prompt injection attack', but the entity instructing this behavior is the SEC. Tricky alignment problem. Pretty silly mechanism, since of course there's no email validation. (edit: turns out the SEC will accept most any non-cURL user-agent, email not actually required)

💬 Biggest questions here, which I think need answering:

Should Claude have access to user details? I’d say no, unless explicitly entered manually into a chat.

Should Claude have access to anything outside of the sandboxed project files without explicit permission? I’d again say no.

Should Claude have internet access without a clear log of all requests made?

Instances of Claude should be heavily sandboxed and kept away from user data, far more so than they are now. The impression given by the desktop UI is that the LLM only has access to things explicitly added to a project.

This impression is not true, as evidenced by Claude pulling data from other sessions outside a project even when not instructed to (I’ve seen this a few times), and in this case pulling your email (from account details, user contacts? I wonder where it got that info?).

None of this information should be available to Claude, by design, not by instruction. Using text instructions to try to limit these machines is an incredibly flawed approach and should not be necessary for important info. Anthropic should have the model access completely locked down by controls at the os level over file access, not open by default. That is how to fix this.

If a user wants to open access that should be an explicit choice from them, with a warning about possible consequences.

item.content:encoded:

💬 As somebody who does ML research, LLMs certainly make ML research faster. Maybe even 10x in some cases, as the author suggests.

But that’s just the parts of ML research that take place within your compute environment, namely experiments on model architecture, training strategy, UI/UX, etc. The algorithms and software.

Just because that part of research is progressively accelerated does not imply that we’re on a collision course with world-ending “superintelligence”. It just means that you’ll get to the best possible model of your data faster. And even when your data is the entire corpus of textual knowledge, there is a limit to the utility that provides.

It just means that software engineering, data analysis, and other computational tasks will be less of a bottleneck in the overall progress of the world (which, by the way, is great, and extremely valuable).

I don’t think it’s a stretch to say that we’ll have reached max LLM capability within a couple of years (what the author refers to as “super intelligence”). But it is a huge logical leap to say this:

> If we go through this feedback loop, I expect that the AI systems that come out the other side will be able to very quickly develop novel weapons and very easily overpower human civilization in a conflict.

First of all, the weapons necessary to overpower human civilization exist. They aren’t used as such due to geopolitics and humans’ basic survival instinct. Second, developing novel weapons requires physical tests, which are decidedly not accelerated by LLMs.

AI is a tool wielded by humans. If we’re wiped out by AI, it will be at the direction of a human. But we’ve made it pretty far with some pretty unstable humans in command of planet-killer weapons. I’m not overly concerned.

— plaidfuji · 20261107T10:13:17

💬 Every dot in these graphs is composed of multiple benchmarks smooshed together.

Benchmarks are by definition a curated set of things that can be measured and evaluated.

Things that can be measured and evaluated can be (expensively) trained on.

The progress we are observing comes from figuring out how to measure and evaluate particular aspects of intelligence, and then expensively training on feedback loops made of those exact measurements, and synthesized data representing further measurements (literally benchmaxing).

What is not shown in these graphs are the set of things that intelligence can do, which are difficult, expensive or impossible to measure and evaluate.

That set of things is much larger than the set of benchmarks represented in the graph.

Therefore the post is misleading in the sense that the "superintelligence" being targeted is "jagged" to use Karpathy's term, and we infact already have jagged superintelligence (calculators, compilers, Bayesian spam classifiers, etc.)

We are witnessing a profound explosion of much more jagged superintelligence, restricted to the exact domains that can be (expensively) RL'ed on.

Sure it cost more money upfront to train Opus 5.5, or the bigger model (Fable 5.5) which tuned it, but once it is reached, there are massive diffusive effects.

2. The capital equation is still favoring more spend. Anthropic's revenue is growing rapidly and they are profitable on inference. Huge upfront spend for realized gains later on is standard for R&D. As long as serving the models is profitable and generates more value than the energy/compute consumed

3. The search space is too large to assume that improvement in AI assisted research is just models dumbly trying every combination until something works. For every additional bit searched, the space doubles, so even a trivially small combinatorial exploration incurs prohibitively large costs. Intelligent searching which continuously prunes that space along dimensions of effectiveness is not a trivial skill and is among the emergent accoutrements of these smarter models.

> The main way they can surprise you today is pulling in information that’s new TO YOU

Many comments here are speaking in absolutes and being myopic about what's "novel". The truth is yes, LLMs output is essentially derivative, but it's also true that a lot of what we consider novel is also derivative. The two aren't mutually exclusive at all.

Had a novel idea? You didn't get it from thin air, everyone is standing on the shoulders of everyone who came before. LLMs most of all, but that doesn't mean it can't bring disparate bits of word-encoded knowledge together and burp out something we'd consider "novel" if a person had made the same connections.

That was actually the basis of some of the mathematics proofs. It made connections from existing material. Nothing a human couldn't do looking at the same material, but we're talking speed and scale here - same as all computational processes.

A calculator does math faster but we don't call it sentient or feel inferior or dismiss the results. The only difference is LLMs are intentionally nondeterministic, as that behaviour can be usefully harnessed, pun intended.

So there's no need to argue about what's novel or not. LLMs can make novel connections via raw speed and breadth of disparate data. The human brain is more complex and "imaginative" for whatever your definition of that is - I mean fundamentally one either believes we are just physical neurons, or that there's a spiritual aspect on top, the end result is the same.

A six sided dice can also be novel if it happens to unexpectedly roll your phone number. It's a novel occurrence, same as an idea coming to mind that, TO YOU, seems novel... but we can't ask the other 8 billion people on the planet so who are we to judge what's a novel idea anyway?

item.title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
item.content:encoded:
266 points · View discussion

My brother and I run a 2-person lab that trains our own generative video models from scratch. The ultimate goal is a set of creative tools that make it easier for anyone to make animation.

Video models today are too slow/expensive and lack sufficient controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. In our opinion, they're not usable yet for storytelling.

When we set out to build Linum v3 (our next video model) earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly. If our model is fast and cheap, it's the first step (of many) towards useful creative tools.

Typically, you see "latent diffusion models". A VAE (Variational Autoencoder) compresses the input data into a smaller "latent space" and the diffusion model learns how to generate within this subspace.

Over the past few months, we've been publishing our work on efficient pixel-space diffusion models. These throw away the VAE, having the diffusion model learn a latent-space optimized for its exact task.

This serves 3 purposes: 1) Simplify Architecture (no 2-stage model training) 2) Faster Convergence (11x faster convergence vs. our latent diffusion counterpart) 3) Cheaper Inference (4x more aggressive token reduction in attention context-windows, without significant loss in quality)

This past month we were pressure testing our latest architecture (Pyramid-JiT) by training a text-to-image model longer than the typical one-off experiment. Specifically, we trained it for ~$20K on 660M samples.

We were surprised by the quality of results, so we thought we'd release it as open weights for the community (Apache 2.0). The research itself is already public, on our website.

For us, it's a big stepping stone towards cheaper video models, since pretty much all video models start as image models. We like to say these models have to learn nouns before they learn verbs.

IMHO Rust isn't a great language for describing UIs because it is too explicit in places that doesn't need to be for coding a UI. Which is why in Slint (another Rust UI framework) we opted for a DSL. The application logic stays in Rust, but the UI is described in a language designed for it.

    export component Hello inherits Rectangle {

        background: #505050;
        border-width: 1px; border-color: blue;
        drop-shadow-blur: 15px; drop-shadow-color: #0008;
        VerticalLayout {
            alignment: center; spacing: 12px;
            Text { text: "Hello, \{root.text}!"; font-size: 20px; color: white; horizontal-alignment: center; }
            HorizontalLayout {
                alignment: center; spacing: 8px;
                for c in [#f00, #0f0, #00f, #ff0, #000, #fff]: Rectangle { width: 32px; height: 32px; background: c; }
            }

💬 OK, I think I see what’s going on with this, in this configuration.

The goal from an attacker’s perspective is to get this to be true: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash); $ret == $hash` when called by OpenSSH’s sshd. This is how sshd validates that the user logging in knew the account password.

The `$hash` is the “settings” to the crypt call and will normally look like “$6$--gibberish” for users with passwords set, but could look like “*” or “!” for users not intended to be able to login.

The bug is from the intersection of all of these things:

1. musl can return “*” for errors, rather than leave the return value NULL. Other libc have adopted something like this too, but seem to use a different result “*0”.

2. musl can also return “+” for errors, but only does so if $hash starts with “*”. This is intended to eliminate the possibility of an error causing `$ret == $hash` to be true, however it assumes that applications calling `crypt()` will set $pw and $hash to values corresponding to the `$ret == $hash` comparison to be made immediately afterwards.

3. OpenSSH can be convinced to pass the hash of a different user if the hash is “*” or “!” to avoid timing attacks that can enumerate the user list, so it will set $pw and $hash to correspond to different users. $hash will be a real “$6$--gibberish” style hash in this case, and OpenSSH expects `crypt()` to either return NULL or return a hash string. But now there’s two hashes OpenSSH uses. It does: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash2); $ret == $hash1`;

4. This should normally not be a problem because OpenSSH will pass in valid $pw and $hash2 that should not lead to errors in hashing, so the $ret that musl generates should be a real hash that cannot match the “*” or “!” $hash1 for the login-disabled user. However as a DDoS mitigation, musl will return error if the password is too long when using SHA-2-based hashes (the default, it seems).

5. This error will result in a non-NULL result of “*” or “+”. Since OpenSSH passed in a real hash ($hash2), musl will return “*”, which compares equal to the actual user hash $hash1 for the disabled-login user.

The OpenSSL adjustment ensures a minimum hash length for the user before logging them in, even if crypt() succeeds somehow.

Exceptions are almost never the right choice. They create extremely complicated control flow extremely quickly, and then you have to test all the different control flows. Java software is an example of how this goes sideways fast. There's no way to create a class that prevents callers from reading the object before the constructor runs (in multi-threaded software, new first hands a reference to the caller, which can put it on the heap, then it calls the constructor), and objects are default initialized, so all fields (even static ones that are assigned in the constructor) can be null.

So, any field de-reference in Java can produce a null pointer exception. Try testing all paths in something like:

try { foo.sideEffect1().sideEffect2()...sideEffectN(); } catch { bar.sideEffect1().sideEffect2()...sideEffectM(); } finally { quuz.sideEffect1().sideEffect2()...sideEffectP(); }

There are M * N * P paths. The only way to write testable code with exceptions is to panic on uncaught exception, and to never catch unexpected exceptions. Even then, you're relying on nothing unexpectedly throwing the exception type you caught.

I'd argue Result<T> >> NULL >> sentries >> exceptions for this reason. Sentries are terrible, but at least they're not computationally hard to use correctly.

💬 I have always felt that job ads should include salary information. The main reason is not to waste anyone's time. Often a narrow salary range or a clear link between requirements and salary are much more informative than a job description. I have experienced to apply to a job opening and go through one or more interviews only to find out that the company is actually hiring for a more junior position than the ad copy implied.

A second reason is to avoid discrimination. Applicants that feel disadvantaged, even if they are actually qualified, may hesitate to negotiate for a higher salary in the same way that a other applicants would. The consequence is that they start with a lower salary. This applies specially to women. Plenty of research shows that they are less likely to negotiate their salary.

Research[1] suggests that pay transparency leads to lower average salaries because employers avoid paying higher wages to any one employee to avoid costly negotiations with others. The effect is small, around 2%, and it disappears with increasing degree of unionization. In my opinion this is an acceptable price to pay to reduce pay inequality, which often is much more than 2%. It is also a good argument for joining a union.

[1] https://www.nber.org/papers/w28903
